pages.question: A 48-year-old woman with a 6-year history of serotonegative rheumatoid arthritis presents for a follow-up visit. She is currently on methotrexate 15 mg weekly and reports persistent joint swelling in her hands and morning stiffness lasting approximately 90 minutes. Her CRP is 3.8 mg/L (reference < 1.0 mg/L) and ESR is 54 mm/hr. She asks whether dietary changes could help reduce her inflammation. A detailed diet history reveals high consumption of fast food, white bread, sugary beverages, and packaged snacks. Which of the following dietary interventions has the strongest evidence for reducing systemic inflammatory markers in patients with rheumatoid arthritis?

answers.text: Eliminate all dietary fats to prevent pro-inflammatory eicosanoid synthesis
Recommend a gluten-free diet to reduce joint inflammation
Advise increased consumption of corn oil and sunflower oil to replace saturated animal fats
Transition to a Mediterranean dietary pattern emphasizing vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, olive oil, and fatty fish
Initiate a high-protein, low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine production

pages.question: A 48-year-old woman with a 6-year history of serotonegative rheumatoid arthritis presents for a follow-up visit. She is currently on methotrexate 15 mg weekly and reports persistent joint swelling in her hands and morning stiffness lasting approximately 90 minutes. Her CRP is 3.8 mg/L (reference < 1.0 mg/L) and ESR is 54 mm/hr. She asks whether dietary changes could help reduce her inflammation. A detailed diet history reveals high consumption of fast food, white bread, sugary beverages, and packaged snacks. Which of the following dietary interventions has the strongest evidence for reducing systemic inflammatory markers in patients with rheumatoid arthritis?

answers.text:
Eliminate all dietary fats to prevent pro-inflammatory eicosanoid synthesis
(0%)

Recommend a gluten-free diet to reduce joint inflammation
(0%)

Advise increased consumption of corn oil and sunflower oil to replace saturated animal fats
(0%)

Transition to a Mediterranean dietary pattern emphasizing vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, olive oil, and fatty fish
(100%)

Initiate a high-protein, low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine production
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The Mediterranean diet, rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, olive oil, and fish, has the strongest evidence for reducing systemic inflammatory markers such as CRP and ESR in rheumatoid arthritis. Ultraprocessed foods and refined sugars promote inflammation via activation of NF-κB and increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, worsening disease activity. Dietary modification should be considered a complementary strategy alongside pharmacologic management.
(Choice A)
Eliminate all dietary fats to prevent pro-inflammatory eicosanoid synthesis
Eliminating all dietary fats is neither safe nor effective. Many fatty acids, including omega-3 fatty acids found in fish and flaxseed, are anti-inflammatory and beneficial in RA. This approach would also lead to deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and essential fatty acids, causing additional harm. The goal is to shift the fat composition toward anti-inflammatory sources, not eliminate fat entirely.
(Choice B)
Recommend a gluten-free diet to reduce joint inflammation
A gluten-free diet is medically indicated only for patients with celiac disease or confirmed non-celiac gluten sensitivity. There is no established evidence that gluten elimination reduces inflammation in serotonegative rheumatoid arthritis patients without concurrent gluten-related disorders. Furthermore, many commercially available gluten-free products are highly processed and may actually worsen dietary quality by increasing refined starches and sugars while reducing fiber intake. This approach is not supported by rheumatology or nutrition guidelines for RA management.
(Choice C)
Advise increased consumption of corn oil and sunflower oil to replace saturated animal fats
Corn oil and sunflower oil are predominantly high in omega-6 fatty acids (linoleic acid), which serve as precursors to arachidonic acid and pro-inflammatory eicosanoids such as prostaglandin E2 and leukotriene B4. Increasing omega-6 intake without a corresponding increase in omega-3 fatty acids worsens the omega-6:omega-3 ratio and promotes systemic inflammation. These oils are not appropriate anti-inflammatory dietary substitutions in RA.
(Choice D)
Transition to a Mediterranean dietary pattern emphasizing vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, olive oil, and fatty fish
The Mediterranean diet has the most robust evidence for reducing systemic inflammatory markers in rheumatoid arthritis. It is rich in omega-3 fatty acids (from fatty fish), polyphenols, fiber, and monounsaturated fats, all of which downregulate pro-inflammatory pathways including NF-κB activation and reduce production of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6. Conversely, the patient's current diet—high in ultraprocessed foods, refined sugars, and saturated fats—promotes inflammation through increased arachidonic acid metabolism and oxidative stress. Clinical studies have demonstrated reductions in CRP, ESR, and disease activity scores (DAS28) with adherence to the Mediterranean diet. This dietary pattern also supports cardiovascular health, which is particularly important in RA patients who carry elevated cardiovascular risk. Dietary counseling should be integrated into the overall management plan as a safe, evidence-based adjunct to pharmacotherapy.
(Choice E)
Initiate a high-protein, low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine production
While ketogenic diets may reduce some inflammatory markers in certain populations, the evidence specifically in rheumatoid arthritis is limited and inconsistent. Most studies showing anti-inflammatory effects of ketogenic diets have been in epilepsy, obesity, or metabolic syndrome rather than autoimmune conditions. Additionally, this dietary pattern is difficult to sustain long-term and lacks the comprehensive anti-inflammatory nutrient profile of the Mediterranean diet. Current RA management guidelines do not recommend ketogenic diets as a first-line dietary intervention.

pages.question:
A 55-year-old male presents with severe and persistent abdominal pain that has been ongoing for over four months. The pain is strong, rated at 8/10, continuous, and gets relief with over-the-counter acid reducers. He reports some constipation, but no weight loss or change in appetite has been noted. His family history reveals his mother had peptic ulcer disease, but she never received treatment. He works as a financial analyst, frequently faces stress at work, and feels burdened by tight deadlines. Vital signs show a temperature of 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure 128/80 mm Hg, heart rate 76/min, and respirations 16/min. The abdominal examination reveals normal bowel sounds and tenderness in the upper middle section of the stomach. No mass can be felt, but stool tests show hidden blood presence. Laboratory workup indicates:  

Sodium 139 mEq/L
Potassium 4.0 mEq/L
Chloride 102 mEq/L
Bicarbonate 26 mEq/L
Calcium 11.8 mg/dL
Phosphorus 2.0 mg/dL
BUN 35 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL

What is the most probable diagnosis among the following options?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The combination of hypercalcemia (11.8 mg/dL) and refractory peptic ulcer disease with occult GI bleeding strongly suggests MEN Type 1. This syndrome typically involves parathyroid adenomas (causing hypercalcemia), pancreatic islet cell tumors (potentially gastrinomas causing Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), and pituitary adenomas.
(Choice A)
Peptic ulcer disease
While peptic ulcer disease could explain the abdominal pain and positive stool guaiac, it would not account for the hypercalcemia (11.8 mg/dL). The combination of refractory peptic ulcer disease with hypercalcemia suggests an underlying endocrine disorder rather than simple peptic ulcer disease.
(Choice B)
Insulinoma
Insulinoma typically presents with Whipple's triad (symptoms of hypoglycemia, documented low blood glucose, and relief with glucose administration). This patient has no hypoglycemic symptoms and the laboratory findings show hypercalcemia, which is not associated with insulinoma.
(Choice C)
Hypervitaminosis A
Hypervitaminosis A can cause hypercalcemia, but typically presents with hepatomegaly, skin changes, hair loss, and bone pain. It would not explain the constellation of refractory peptic ulcer disease with occult GI bleeding in this clinical context.
(Choice D)
Parathyroid carcinoma
Parathyroid carcinoma can cause severe hypercalcemia, but it typically presents as a palpable neck mass with extremely high calcium levels (often >14 mg/dL). The combination of moderate hypercalcemia with gastrointestinal symptoms suggests a syndrome involving multiple endocrine organs rather than isolated parathyroid malignancy.
(Choice E)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia Type 1
This patient most likely has MEN Type 1, which is characterized by tumors in multiple endocrine organs including parathyroid glands (causing hypercalcemia), pancreatic islet cells (potentially causing Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with refractory peptic ulcers), and pituitary glands. The combination of hypercalcemia and intractable peptic ulcer disease strongly suggests this diagnosis.

pages.question: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to her primary care physician for follow-up. Her HbA1c is 8.2%, BMI is 31 kg/m², and she is currently on metformin. The physician refers her to a registered dietitian nutritionist (RDN) for individualized dietary counseling focused on carbohydrate management and weight reduction. The RDN plans to provide three one-hour sessions of individualized nutritional assessment and intervention over the next month. Which of the following CPT code sets is most appropriate for billing these medical nutrition therapy (MNT) services?

answers.text:
CPT 96150-96155 for health and behavior assessment and intervention services
(85%)

CPT 99401-99404 for preventive medicine counseling and risk factor reduction interventions
(0%)

CPT 97804 for group medical nutrition therapy sessions
(0%)

CPT 97802 for the initial MNT session and CPT 97803 for follow-up MNT sessions
(15%)

CPT 99213 and 99214 for office evaluation and management visits
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Medical nutrition therapy (MNT) for diabetes and other chronic conditions is billed using CPT codes 97802 (initial individual MNT, 15-minute increments) and 97803 (follow-up individual MNT, 15-minute increments). These codes require documentation of a physician referral, a nutrition diagnosis, and the time spent in direct patient contact. Medicare covers up to 3 hours of MNT in the first year for patients with diabetes or renal disease when provided by a qualified RDN.
(Choice A)
CPT 96150-96155 for health and behavior assessment and intervention services
CPT 96150–96155 are health and behavior assessment and intervention codes used primarily by psychologists and other behavioral health providers to address psychological, behavioral, emotional, and social factors affecting physical health. While behavioral factors are relevant to dietary adherence, these codes are not appropriate for RDN-led medical nutrition therapy and would be considered misuse of the coding system in this context.
(Choice B)
CPT 99401-99404 for preventive medicine counseling and risk factor reduction interventions
CPT 99401-99404 are preventive medicine counseling codes used by physicians for general risk factor reduction interventions. While these are time-based codes, they are not specific to medical nutrition therapy and do not capture the specialized nutrition assessment, diagnosis, and intervention framework that qualified RDNs provide for chronic disease management.
(Choice C)
CPT 97804 for group medical nutrition therapy sessions
CPT 97804 is used for group MNT sessions involving two or more individuals and is billed in 30-minute increments per group member. This code is inappropriate for the individualized, one-on-one sessions described in this scenario. Using group codes for individual sessions would misrepresent the service intensity and could constitute improper billing practices.
(Choice D)
CPT 97802 for the initial MNT session and CPT 97803 for follow-up MNT sessions
CPT 97802 (Medical Nutrition Therapy, initial assessment and intervention, individual, face-to-face with the patient, each 15 minutes) is used for the first individualized MNT encounter, while CPT 97803 (reassessment and intervention, individual, face-to-face, each 15 minutes) is used for subsequent follow-up sessions. These codes are specifically designed for MNT services provided by a qualified RDN and are billed in 15-minute increments, so a 60-minute initial session would be billed as four units of 97802. Medicare Part B covers up to 3 hours of MNT in the first year and 2 hours per year thereafter for patients with diabetes mellitus or chronic kidney disease, provided there is a physician referral. Documentation must include the nutrition diagnosis using the Nutrition Care Process, goals set, interventions provided, and time spent. Proper use of these codes ensures appropriate reimbursement and supports the role of the RDN in chronic disease management.
(Choice E)
CPT 99213 and 99214 for office evaluation and management visits
Evaluation and management (E/M) codes such as 99213 and 99214 are used by physicians and other qualified healthcare professionals for office visits involving medical decision-making. These codes are not appropriate for billing individualized nutritional counseling sessions provided by an RDN, which require nutrition-specific coding that captures the specialized assessment and intervention framework of medical nutrition therapy.

pages.question: A 48-year-old man presents for a routine physical examination. He has no known medical history and takes no medications. He works as an accountant and describes a sedentary lifestyle with minimal physical activity. He eats primarily fast food and processed snacks. On examination, his blood pressure is 134/86 mmHg, height is 5'10', weight is 218 lbs, and waist circumference is 106 cm. Laboratory studies show fasting glucose 108 mg/dL, fasting triglycerides 188 mg/dL, and HDL cholesterol 36 mg/dL. He asks if these results are concerning. Which of the following correctly identifies whether this patient meets diagnostic criteria for metabolic syndrome and specifies the components present?

answers.text:
This patient does not meet criteria for metabolic syndrome because his blood pressure of 134/86 mmHg does not reach the hypertension threshold of 140/90 mmHg required for the blood pressure component
(0%)

This patient does not have metabolic syndrome because his LDL cholesterol was not measured and elevated LDL cholesterol is required as one of the five essential diagnostic components
(33.33%)

This patient meets criteria for prediabetes only based on his fasting glucose of 108 mg/dL and does not have metabolic syndrome because metabolic syndrome requires prediabetes plus at least two additional specific cardiovascular risk factors
(0%)

This patient meets criteria for metabolic syndrome with all five components present: waist circumference >102 cm, triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dL, blood pressure ≥130/85 mmHg, and fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL
(33.33%)

This patient meets criteria for metabolic syndrome with three of five components — elevated triglycerides, low HDL, and elevated fasting glucose — but his waist circumference and blood pressure do not meet thresholds
(33.33%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Metabolic syndrome per NCEP ATP III criteria requires three or more of five components: waist circumference >102 cm in men, triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dL in men, blood pressure ≥130/85 mmHg, and fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL. This patient meets all five criteria and has metabolic syndrome. Recognition triggers first-line lifestyle intervention targeting visceral adiposity.
(Choice A)
This patient does not meet criteria for metabolic syndrome because his blood pressure of 134/86 mmHg does not reach the hypertension threshold of 140/90 mmHg required for the blood pressure component
This answer incorrectly applies the standard hypertension diagnostic threshold instead of the metabolic syndrome-specific blood pressure criterion. The metabolic syndrome blood pressure criterion per NCEP ATP III is ≥130/85 mmHg — not the JNC hypertension diagnostic threshold of ≥140/90 mmHg. The metabolic syndrome criteria use lower thresholds to identify individuals at earlier stages of cardiometabolic risk, before overt hypertension develops. This patient's blood pressure of 134/86 mmHg clearly meets the metabolic syndrome criterion of ≥130/85 mmHg. He meets all five criteria and has metabolic syndrome.
(Choice B)
This patient does not have metabolic syndrome because his LDL cholesterol was not measured and elevated LDL cholesterol is required as one of the five essential diagnostic components
LDL cholesterol is not one of the five components of the NCEP ATP III metabolic syndrome diagnostic criteria. The lipid components of metabolic syndrome are triglycerides (≥150 mg/dL) and HDL cholesterol (low HDL), not LDL. LDL elevation is an independent cardiovascular risk factor managed separately. The five metabolic syndrome components are abdominal obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL, elevated blood pressure, and elevated fasting glucose — none of which includes LDL.
(Choice C)
This patient meets criteria for prediabetes only based on his fasting glucose of 108 mg/dL and does not have metabolic syndrome because metabolic syndrome requires prediabetes plus at least two additional specific cardiovascular risk factors
This answer fundamentally misunderstands the diagnostic framework for metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed by the presence of three or more of five specific, well-defined components — it is not defined as prediabetes plus additional cardiovascular risk factors. While this patient does have prediabetes (fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dL), prediabetes is just one of the five metabolic syndrome components. The diagnosis requires systematically evaluating all five components and counting how many are present. This patient meets all five components and clearly has metabolic syndrome.
(Choice D)
This patient meets criteria for metabolic syndrome with all five components present: waist circumference >102 cm, triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL, HDL <40 mg/dL, blood pressure ≥130/85 mmHg, and fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL
Metabolic syndrome is defined by the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP ATP III) as the presence of three or more of the following five components: (1) Abdominal obesity: waist circumference >102 cm (40 inches) in men or >88 cm (35 inches) in women — this patient's waist is 106 cm, exceeding the threshold; (2) Hypertriglyceridemia: fasting triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL — this patient's triglycerides are 188 mg/dL; (3) Low HDL cholesterol: HDL <40 mg/dL in men or <50 mg/dL in women — this patient's HDL is 36 mg/dL; (4) Elevated blood pressure: ≥130/85 mmHg or on antihypertensive therapy — this patient's BP is 134/86 mmHg; (5) Elevated fasting glucose: ≥100 mg/dL or on antidiabetic therapy — this patient's fasting glucose is 108 mg/dL. This patient meets all five criteria and therefore clearly has metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome confers approximately a two-fold increased risk of cardiovascular disease and a five-fold increased risk of type 2 diabetes compared to individuals without the syndrome. The underlying pathophysiology is visceral adiposity-driven insulin resistance, and first-line management is lifestyle intervention targeting the central adiposity — dietary modification emphasizing reduced refined carbohydrates and saturated fat, and structured physical activity of at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise per week, targeting 5–7% weight loss.
(Choice E)
This patient meets criteria for metabolic syndrome with three of five components — elevated triglycerides, low HDL, and elevated fasting glucose — but his waist circumference and blood pressure do not meet thresholds
This answer incorrectly applies the thresholds for waist circumference and blood pressure. The waist circumference threshold for men is >102 cm — this patient's waist is 106 cm, exceeding the threshold. The blood pressure threshold for metabolic syndrome is ≥130/85 mmHg — this patient's BP is 134/86 mmHg, meeting the criterion. This patient meets all five components, not just three.

pages.question: A 19-year-old college athlete comes to the clinic due to his coach's concern about his temperament during training sessions. His roommate mentions that the patient has been acting increasingly irritable and sometimes aggressive. The young man denies any significant issues but mentions he is aiming to enhance his athletic performance. During examination, he presents with widespread body acne, hair thinning on the scalp, and a noticeable enlargement beneath both nipples. No abnormalities are detected in his heart and lung examination. What is the most probable substance he is using?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The scenario presents classic signs of anabolic steroid use: behavioral changes (increased aggression), dermatologic effects (acne, male pattern baldness), and endocrine disruption (gynecomastia). Anabolic steroids increase testosterone levels, with aromatization of excess testosterone to estrogen causing breast tissue development in males. This substance abuse pattern is commonly seen in athletes seeking to enhance performance or muscle mass.
(Choice A)
Methamphetamine
Methamphetamine can cause severe dermatologic effects including 'meth mouth' and skin picking lesions, but these differ from the acne pattern seen here. Methamphetamine does not cause gynecomastia or male pattern baldness.
(Choice B)
Anabolic steroids
The combination of aggressive behavior, acne, hair thinning, and gynecomastia suggests anabolic steroid use, often associated with increased testosterone conversion to estrogen causing breast tissue enlargement.
(Choice C)
Inhalants
Inhalants can cause acute intoxication and altered mental states, but they do not produce the constellation of androgenic effects (acne, hair loss, gynecomastia) seen in this patient. These physical findings suggest hormonal rather than solvent-based substance use.
(Choice D)
Cocaine
While cocaine can cause aggressive behavior and mood changes, it does not cause the dermatologic changes (acne) or endocrine effects (gynecomastia) seen in this patient. Cocaine's primary effects are cardiovascular and neurological.
(Choice E)
Phencyclidine
PCP (phencyclidine) can cause aggressive, unpredictable behavior and dissociative effects, but it does not cause the androgenic side effects (acne, male pattern baldness) or gynecomastia characteristic of hormonal disruption.

pages.question:
A 58-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes presents to the clinic with a 2-month history of progressive fatigue, persistent constipation, and low mood. She denies significant weight changes but reports occasional bone aches in her legs. Physical examination is unremarkable except for mild pallor. Laboratory findings are shown below. The patient's symptoms of fatigue, constipation, and low mood are most likely attributable to which of the following?



Hemoglobin	10.2 g/dL
Hematocrit	30%
White Blood Cell Count	7.2 x10^3/µL
Platelet Count	250 x10^3/µL
MCV	88 fL
MCH	29 pg
MCHC	33 g/dL
RDW	13%
Neutrophils	60%
Lymphocytes	30%
Monocytes	7%
Eosinophils	2%
Basophils	1%
Sodium	138 mmol/L
Potassium	4.1 mmol/L
Chloride	102 mmol/L
CO2	24 mmol/L
BUN	14 mg/dL
Creatinine	1.6 mg/dL
Glucose	92 mg/dL
Calcium	10.8 mg/dL
Total Protein	7.8 g/dL
Albumin	4.2 g/dL
AST	28 U/L
ALT	32 U/L
Alkaline Phosphatase	85 U/L
Total Bilirubin	0.8 mg/dL
Serum Protein Electrophoresis	Monoclonal spike present
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's fatigue, constipation, and low mood are likely due to mild hypercalcemia associated with multiple myeloma, as indicated by anemia, renal impairment, mildly elevated calcium, bone aches, and monoclonal protein spike.
(Choice A)
Medication side effect
Diabetes medications (metformin, insulin) do not typically cause anemia, renal impairment, monoclonal protein spikes, or the combination of symptoms seen here that suggest an underlying hematologic malignancy.
(Choice B)
Vitamin deficiency
Vitamin deficiencies (particularly B12 or folate) can cause anemia, fatigue, and mood changes, but would not explain the monoclonal protein spike, renal impairment, or the constellation of findings suggesting multiple myeloma.
(Choice C)
Major depressive disorder
While major depressive disorder can cause fatigue and low mood, it would not explain the anemia, monoclonal protein spike, renal impairment, bone aches, or mildly elevated calcium that suggest an underlying hematologic malignancy.
(Choice D)
Dehydration
Dehydration might cause fatigue and constipation but would not explain the anemia, monoclonal protein spike, renal impairment, or bone aches that collectively suggest multiple myeloma rather than simple volume depletion.
(Choice E)
Electrolyte disturbance
Hypercalcemia is the electrolyte disturbance responsible for this patient's fatigue, constipation, and low mood — the classic triad of mild-to-moderate hypercalcemia remembered as "bones, stones, groans, and psychic moans." This patient's calcium of 10.8 mg/dL is mildly elevated above normal (8.5–10.5 mg/dL) in the context of multiple myeloma, suggested by the constellation of normocytic anemia (Hgb 10.2), renal impairment (creatinine 1.6), bone aches, and monoclonal protein spike on SPEP. In myeloma, osteolytic bone destruction releases calcium into the bloodstream. Even mild hypercalcemia can produce the described constitutional symptoms, and calcium is the single electrolyte abnormality present in this patient's labs that accounts for all three symptoms simultaneously.

pages.question: A 62-year-old retired teacher presents with persistent nasal congestion and watery rhinorrhea that worsens when she enters air-conditioned buildings or encounters strong cleaning product smells at home. She reports no improvement with over-the-counter oral antihistamines and denies symptoms of sneezing, ocular itching, or seasonal exacerbations. Examination reveals pale, edematous nasal turbinates without evidence of polyps or purulent discharge. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic therapy?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has nonallergic rhinitis, characterized by nasal congestion and rhinorrhea triggered by irritants like temperature changes and strong odors, without allergic features. Symptoms persist despite oral antihistamines. The first-line treatment is intranasal glucocorticoids.
(Choice A)
Oral leukotriene receptor antagonists
Leukotriene receptor antagonists are used in allergic rhinitis or asthma but have limited efficacy in nonallergic rhinitis.
(Choice B)
Allergen immunotherapy
Allergen immunotherapy (allergy shots or sublingual tablets) is specifically indicated for IgE-mediated allergic rhinitis confirmed by skin testing or serum-specific IgE. This patient's symptoms are triggered by irritants rather than allergens, and she lacks typical allergic features like sneezing and ocular symptoms.
(Choice C)
Intranasal glucocorticoids
Intranasal glucocorticoids are the first-line treatment for nonallergic rhinitis, effectively reducing inflammation and symptoms like congestion and rhinorrhea.
(Choice D)
Oral antihistamines
Oral antihistamines are ineffective for nonallergic rhinitis because this condition is not mediated by histamine release from mast cells. The patient's lack of response to over-the-counter oral antihistamines supports this diagnosis and rules out allergic rhinitis.
(Choice E)
Intranasal decongestants
Intranasal decongestants (oxymetazoline, phenylephrine) provide temporary symptomatic relief through vasoconstriction but are not appropriate as initial therapy. Prolonged use beyond 3-5 days can cause rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion), making symptoms worse.

pages.question: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician's office by her father due to a murmur detected during a routine school health examination. The child is active and playful, with no history of fatigue, cyanosis, or exercise intolerance. On physical examination, she is alert and shows no distress. Her blood pressure is within the normal range. Heart auscultation reveals a soft, grade-2 systolic ejection murmur heard best at the mid-left sternal border. The murmurs intensity varies with the child's position. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This child presents with a classic innocent (functional) murmur, characterized by its soft intensity (grade 2/6), systolic timing, positional variability, and absence of associated symptoms. Innocent murmurs are present in up to 80% of children at some point and are benign findings that require no treatment. The key distinguishing features include grade ≤2/6 intensity, musical or vibratory quality, variation with position/respiration, and normal growth and development. Reassurance of parents and routine follow-up are appropriate, with the expectation that most innocent murmurs resolve by adolescence.
(Choice A)
12-lead ECG
An ECG is not indicated for evaluation of innocent murmurs in asymptomatic children. The normal cardiovascular examination and typical innocent murmur characteristics make further cardiac workup unnecessary.
(Choice B)
Reassurance and follow-up
Correct. Reassurance and observation are appropriate, as the murmur's characteristics are consistent with a harmless murmur.
(Choice C)
Echocardiogram
Echocardiography is reserved for murmurs with concerning features (grade 3 or higher, diastolic murmurs, harsh quality, or associated symptoms). This soft, positional systolic murmur in an asymptomatic child has classic innocent murmur characteristics.
(Choice D)
Stress test
Exercise stress testing is not indicated in asymptomatic children with innocent murmurs. It would only be considered if there were exercise-induced symptoms like chest pain, syncope, or significant exercise intolerance.
(Choice E)
Chest X-ray
Chest X-ray is not indicated for innocent murmurs in asymptomatic children. It would only be considered if there were signs of heart failure, respiratory symptoms, or other concerning features suggesting structural heart disease.

pages.question: A 26-year-old nulliparous woman presents to her gynecologist with a painless lump in her left breast that she first noticed 2 weeks ago during a routine self-breast exam. She has been taking combined oral contraceptives for the past 6 months to manage dysmenorrhea and reports no changes in the lump's size. She denies any nipple discharge, skin dimpling, or family history of breast cancer. Physical examination reveals a 2-cm, firm, well-circumscribed, rubbery, and freely mobile mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast without associated axillary lymphadenopathy or skin changes. Mammography is not performed due to her age, but ultrasound shows a solid, hypoechoic mass with smooth borders. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This young woman with an isolated, firm, mobile, and well-circumscribed breast mass most likely has a fibroadenoma, a benign estrogen-sensitive tumor common in women under 30. It typically presents as a solitary, painless, rubbery mass in the upper outer quadrant and is distinct from malignancies, which are often irregular, fixed, and associated with additional symptoms like lymphadenopathy or discharge.
(Choice A)
Breast lipoma
Lipomas are soft, fatty tumors that are less firm and rubbery compared to fibroadenomas and are not typically hormone-sensitive or located specifically in breast tissue quadrants.
(Choice B)
Phyllodes tumor
Phyllodes tumors are rare fibroepithelial neoplasms that typically present as large (>3-5 cm), rapidly growing masses in women over 35-40 years old. They have a leaf-like microscopic pattern and potential for malignant transformation.
(Choice C)
Fibroadenoma
Fibroadenomas are the most common benign breast tumors in young women, presenting as firm, mobile, well-circumscribed masses that are often estrogen-sensitive and painless.
(Choice D)
Invasive ductal carcinoma
Invasive ductal carcinoma is rare in women under 30 (incidence <1% before age 30) and typically presents as a spiculated, irregular, fixed mass on imaging and examination. The smooth borders and mobile nature make malignancy unlikely in this young patient.
(Choice E)
Simple breast cyst
Simple breast cysts are fluid-filled lesions that appear anechoic on ultrasound with posterior acoustic enhancement, not solid and hypoechoic as described. They may fluctuate with menstrual cycles and are often tender.

pages.question: A 28-year-old male visits your clinic for an annual examination. He reports feeling perfectly healthy and has a clean bill of past medical history. Currently, he is not on any medications and has no history of substance abuse. His recorded blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg and heart rate is 75/min. During a routine cardiac examination, an early diastolic murmur is heard at the upper right sternal border. What is the most appropriate next step in the management?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
An early diastolic murmur at the upper right sternal border requires further evaluation with transthoracic echocardiography. Unlike systolic murmurs which may be benign, diastolic murmurs are pathological until proven otherwise and typically indicate underlying valvular disease such as aortic regurgitation. Echocardiography is the first-line, non-invasive diagnostic tool to assess valve structure, function, and severity of any regurgitation.
(Choice A)
Chest MRI
While cardiac MRI provides excellent detailed imaging of cardiac structures and can evaluate valve disease, it is not the first-line investigation for newly discovered heart murmurs. Echocardiography is more accessible, cost-effective, and provides adequate initial assessment of valvular abnormalities.
(Choice B)
Transthoracic Echocardiography
Transthoracic Echocardiography (Choice D) is a non-invasive, effective first-line tool for evaluating heart murmurs. It helps identify the structural basis of a murmur and its severity.
(Choice C)
CT Angiography
CT angiography is primarily used to evaluate coronary arteries and is typically reserved for suspected coronary artery disease or acute coronary syndromes. It involves radiation exposure and contrast administration, making it inappropriate as a first-line test for valve assessment in a young, asymptomatic patient with a diastolic murmur.
(Choice D)
Reassurance with no further tests
Diastolic murmurs are pathological until proven otherwise and require further evaluation. Unlike soft systolic murmurs which can be benign (functional), diastolic murmurs typically indicate underlying structural heart disease such as aortic or pulmonary regurgitation. Therefore, reassurance without investigation would be inappropriate.
(Choice E)
24-hour Holter monitor
A Holter monitor is used for detecting intermittent arrhythmias over 24-48 hour periods, not for evaluating structural heart disease. While this patient has a diastolic murmur suggesting possible valvular pathology, a Holter monitor would not provide information about valve structure or function.

pages.question: A 4-year-old girl who recently immigrated from a region with limited access to healthcare is brought to the emergency department with acute onset of high fever, severe sore throat, excessive drooling, and a muffled voice. She appears toxic and is sitting forward with her neck extended to ease breathing. Her parents confirm she has not received any childhood vaccinations due to unavailability in their home country. Which of the following is the most significant risk factor for her condition?

answers.text:
Frequent attendance at group childcare settings
(1.82%)

Preceding viral upper respiratory tract infection
(5.45%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Acute epiglottitis is a potentially life-threatening condition most commonly caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) in unvaccinated children. The widespread implementation of Hib vaccination has dramatically reduced the incidence of this condition. Lack of Hib vaccination is the most significant modifiable risk factor, far outweighing environmental exposures or comorbid conditions.
(Choice A)
Underlying allergic rhinitis
Allergic rhinitis causes chronic nasal inflammation but does not predispose to acute bacterial epiglottitis. The primary risk factor remains lack of Hib immunization.
(Choice B)
Exposure to household pets
While pets can transmit certain infections, they are not a primary risk factor for epiglottitis, which is mainly bacterial and linked to Hib.
(Choice C)
Lack of recommended immunizations
Incompletely vaccinated children are at highest risk for epiglottitis due to Haemophilus influenzae type b, as the Hib vaccine provides strong protection against this pathogen.
(Choice D)
Frequent attendance at group childcare settings
While group childcare settings increase exposure risk for Haemophilus influenzae type b transmission, the absence of Hib vaccination remains the most significant modifiable risk factor for developing epiglottitis.
(Choice E)
Preceding viral upper respiratory tract infection
Viral upper respiratory infections can create mucosal inflammation that may facilitate secondary bacterial invasion, but this is a less significant risk factor than unvaccinated status for Hib epiglottitis.

pages.question: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being involved in a high-speed motorcycle accident. She complains of severe pain in her right arm and inability to extend her wrist or fingers. Physical examination reveals swelling, ecchymosis, and deformity in the midportion of the right humerus. She has a wrist drop on the affected side, and the radial pulse is absent on the right but present on the left. Sensation is intact in all dermatomes. X-ray confirms a displaced midshaft fracture of the right humerus. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient's injury?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has a midshaft humeral fracture with evidence of radial nerve injury and vascular compromise (absent radial pulse). Most midshaft humeral fractures are treated nonsurgically, but neurovascular compromise is an indication for open reduction and surgical exploration.
(Choice A)
Observation and pain management only
Observation with pain management alone would be inappropriate for any displaced fracture, but is particularly dangerous in this case due to the absent radial pulse indicating vascular injury that could lead to limb ischemia and permanent damage if not surgically addressed.
(Choice B)
Intramedullary nailing without vascular exploration
Intramedullary nailing may be used for some humeral fractures, but without exploration, the vascular compromise would not be addressed, making this inappropriate.
(Choice C)
Closed reduction and coaptation splint
Closed reduction and splinting are appropriate for many stable midshaft humeral fractures without neurovascular compromise. However, this patient's absent radial pulse indicates vascular injury that requires immediate surgical exploration and repair.
(Choice D)
Functional bracing with sling immobilization
Functional bracing with sling immobilization is an effective nonsurgical treatment for stable, minimally displaced midshaft humeral fractures without neurovascular complications. This patient's absent radial pulse indicates vascular compromise that necessitates immediate surgical intervention.
(Choice E)
Open reduction and surgical exploration
Open reduction and surgical exploration are indicated due to the neurovascular compromise evidenced by the absent radial pulse, in addition to the radial nerve palsy and significant fracture displacement.

pages.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist with complaints of persistent fatigue, mild weight gain of 3 kg over the past two months, occasional nausea, and bilateral breast tenderness. She has a history of endometriosis and started depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injections 4 months ago for contraception and symptom management. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago, and she reports no recent sexual activity but admits to inconsistent condom use earlier. She is concerned these symptoms indicate a serious side effect of the medication and asks about switching to another form of birth control. Vital signs are normal, and physical examination reveals mild breast engorgement without masses. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text:
Measure serum follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone levels
(4.84%)

Switch to a combined oral contraceptive pill
(0%)

Reassure the patient and continue current DMPA regimen
(6.45%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) can lead to amenorrhea and side effects mimicking early pregnancy, such as fatigue, weight gain, nausea, and breast tenderness. In a woman of childbearing age with absence of menses for over 1 month and these symptoms, pregnancy must be ruled out via a urine pregnancy test before considering changes in contraception or further evaluation.
(Choice A)
Measure serum follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone levels
FSH and LH levels could help evaluate secondary amenorrhea causes such as hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction, but pregnancy remains the most common and immediately treatable cause of amenorrhea in reproductive-aged women. These hormone levels would be appropriate after pregnancy is definitively excluded.
(Choice B)
Order a pelvic ultrasound
While pelvic ultrasound would be valuable if pregnancy is confirmed or other gynecologic pathology is suspected, it is not the most appropriate initial step. A urine pregnancy test is more cost-effective, immediately available, and sufficient to rule out the most likely diagnosis in this clinical scenario.
(Choice C)
Switch to a combined oral contraceptive pill
Switching contraceptive methods without first confirming non-pregnant status is contraindicated, as combined oral contraceptives contain estrogen which is teratogenic in early pregnancy. The diagnostic workup must exclude pregnancy before any contraceptive changes are considered.
(Choice D)
Reassure the patient and continue current DMPA regimen
Reassurance without ruling out pregnancy is inappropriate given the constellation of symptoms (fatigue, weight gain, nausea, breast tenderness) and 7-week amenorrhea. While DMPA can cause similar symptoms, pregnancy is a critical differential that must be excluded first in any woman of reproductive age with amenorrhea.
(Choice E)
Administer a urine pregnancy test
This is the correct next step. The patient's symptoms and amenorrhea could indicate pregnancy, which must be excluded before attributing them to DMPA side effects or proceeding with management changes.

pages.question: A 42-year-old man with a 5-year history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of progressive weakness in his right arm and leg, accompanied by numbness and tingling. He reports difficulty walking and has fallen twice. His last exacerbation was 18 months ago, treated successfully with intravenous corticosteroids. Neurological examination reveals 3/5 strength in the right upper and lower extremities, hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign on the right. MRI of the brain shows new gadolinium-enhancing lesions in the left cerebral hemisphere. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient's condition?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of multiple sclerosis (MS), characterized by new neurological deficits and corresponding MRI findings of active demyelinating lesions. High-dose intravenous glucocorticoids, such as methylprednisolone, are the first-line treatment for acute MS exacerbations with disabling symptoms. Plasma exchange is reserved for cases refractory to glucocorticoids.
(Choice A)
Intravenous methylprednisolone
High-dose intravenous glucocorticoids like methylprednisolone are the standard first-line treatment for acute exacerbations of MS to reduce inflammation and shorten the duration of the relapse.
(Choice B)
Intravenous natalizumab
Natalizumab is a disease-modifying agent for MS, administered for long-term control, but it is not used for acute management of exacerbations.
(Choice C)
Oral prednisone
Oral glucocorticoids are less effective than high-dose intravenous formulations for acute MS exacerbations and are not recommended as first-line therapy.
(Choice D)
Intravenous immunoglobulin
Intravenous immunoglobulin lacks evidence for efficacy in treating acute MS exacerbations and is not part of standard treatment algorithms for multiple sclerosis relapses.
(Choice E)
Observation and supportive care
Observation without active treatment is inappropriate for acute MS exacerbations with disabling neurological symptoms like significant weakness and falls, as immediate intervention with IV corticosteroids can shorten relapse duration and improve recovery.

pages.question: A 32-year-old man presents to the clinic with a severe, throbbing headache localized to the right temple that began 4 hours ago. He reports similar episodes occurring 2-3 times per month, often triggered by high-stress periods at work or when he skips meals due to a busy schedule. Today, he has been fasting intermittently for weight loss and notes feeling dehydrated after a long day without adequate fluid intake. The pain is accompanied by nausea and sensitivity to light, but he denies fever, neck stiffness, or visual changes. Vital signs are normal, and neurologic examination reveals no focal deficits. He took 1000 mg of acetaminophen 1 hour ago without significant relief. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient presents with episodic, unilateral throbbing headache consistent with migraine, likely triggered by stress, fasting, and dehydration. His symptoms are refractory to initial acetaminophen, warranting escalation to a triptan such as sumatriptan for acute management. Neuroimaging, lumbar puncture, antibiotics, and oxygen therapy are not indicated given the normal vital signs, absence of red flags, and classic migraine features.
(Choice A)
Oral sumatriptan
Sumatriptan is appropriate for acute migraine management in cases refractory to simple analgesia like acetaminophen.
(Choice B)
High-flow oxygen therapy
High-flow oxygen therapy is the first-line abortive treatment for cluster headaches, not migraines. This patient's presentation lacks classic cluster headache features such as periorbital pain, lacrimation, nasal congestion, or the characteristic circadian timing. The unilateral throbbing pain with photophobia and nausea is typical of migraine.
(Choice C)
Lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture is not indicated as this patient lacks signs of meningitis (fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status) or subarachnoid hemorrhage (sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache, neurologic deficits). The gradual onset and episodic nature with known triggers point to primary headache disorder.
(Choice D)
CT scan of the head
CT scan is not indicated for this patient with typical migraine features and normal neurologic examination. Neuroimaging would be appropriate if there were red flags such as sudden onset ('thunderclap' headache), focal neurologic deficits, altered mental status, fever with neck stiffness, or change in headache pattern in patients over 50.
(Choice E)
Intravenous antibiotics
Antibiotics are not indicated as there are no signs of bacterial infection such as fever, neck stiffness, or altered mental status that would suggest meningitis or other CNS infection. This presentation is consistent with primary migraine headache.

pages.question: A 32-year-old patient assigned female at birth presents to a primary care clinic complaining of longstanding emotional distress and discomfort with their physical appearance. The patient reports that since early adolescence, they have felt a strong sense of being male and have been deeply troubled by the development of breasts and menstrual cycles, which they perceive as incongruent with their inner sense of self. They express a persistent desire to live as a man, including pursuing chest masculinization surgery and hormone therapy to deepen their voice and promote facial hair growth. The patient denies hallucinations or delusions but endorses occasional low mood related to these concerns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's persistent distress due to incongruence between their gender identity (male) and assigned gender (female), along with discomfort from secondary sexual characteristics, meets criteria for gender dysphoria. Key diagnostic features include: (1) marked incongruence between experienced and assigned gender lasting ≥6 months, (2) clinically significant distress or impairment, and (3) desire for gender-affirming interventions. Gender dysphoria should be distinguished from gender nonconformity (no distress about gender identity) and body dysmorphic disorder (focus on perceived physical flaws rather than gender identity). Management includes psychological support, hormone therapy, and surgical interventions as appropriate, with screening for common comorbid conditions like depression and anxiety.
(Choice A)
Gender dysphoria
This is the correct diagnosis, as the patient's symptoms align with persistent incongruence between gender identity and assigned gender, causing significant distress and a desire for gender-affirming interventions.
(Choice B)
Body dysmorphic disorder
Body dysmorphic disorder involves preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear minor to others. Unlike gender dysphoria, BDD does not involve incongruence between gender identity and assigned gender, and the distress focuses on specific body parts rather than overall gender identity.
(Choice C)
Gender nonconformity
Gender nonconformity refers to behaviors, interests, or appearance that do not conform to cultural expectations for one's assigned gender. Crucially, it does not involve distress about one's gender identity or the desire for gender-affirming medical interventions, which distinguishes it from gender dysphoria.
(Choice D)
Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia involves psychotic symptoms like hallucinations or delusions, which are absent here; the patient's concerns are focused on gender identity without evidence of psychosis.
(Choice E)
Major depressive disorder
While the patient reports occasional low mood, this appears to be secondary to gender-related distress rather than representing a primary major depressive episode. Major depressive disorder requires persistent depressed mood or anhedonia with additional neurovegetative symptoms that are not described here.

pages.question: A long-term prospective study was designed to evaluate the association between chronic high sugar beverage consumption and the prevalence of type 2 diabetes in middle-aged men. A sample of men aged 35-60 was chosen. Their daily intake of sugary drinks was calculated at the start using a detailed dietary survey, and the group was observed for an eight-year period for the onset of diabetes. The findings indicated that men with high initial sugar beverage consumption had three times the rate of developing type 2 diabetes over eight years compared to those with low consumption (RR = 3.0, 95% CI = 1.2 - 5.3). According to the study's findings, what percentage of type 2 diabetes in men with high sugar intake is attributable to their consumption?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
In this fictitious study, ARP is obtained by calculating the excess risk tied to sugar consumption among the cohort's development of diabetes. With an RR of 3.0, the ARP is (3.0 - 1)/3.0, which equals 67%. This suggests that high sugar intake accounts for 67% of the diabetes cases among the higher intake group, presenting a significant dietary risk factor.
(Choice A)
67%
Here, ARP = (3.0 - 1)/3.0 = 0.67 (67%). As per the study, 67% of diabetes in the high intake group is due to high sugar beverage consumption.
(Choice B)
80%
This is incorrect. The ARP formula is (RR - 1)/RR. With RR = 3.0, this gives us (3.0 - 1)/3.0 = 2.0/3.0 = 0.67 or 67%. The value 80% significantly overestimates the attributable risk percent.
(Choice C)
55%
This is incorrect. Using the ARP formula (RR - 1)/RR with the given RR of 3.0: (3.0 - 1)/3.0 = 2.0/3.0 = 0.67 or 67%. The value 55% does not result from this calculation.
(Choice D)
30%
This is incorrect. The attributable risk percent (ARP) is calculated as (RR - 1)/RR. With RR = 3.0, the calculation is (3.0 - 1)/3.0 = 2.0/3.0 = 0.67 or 67%, not 30%.
(Choice E)
95%
This is incorrect. The ARP is calculated as (RR - 1)/RR = (3.0 - 1)/3.0 = 0.67 or 67%. A value of 95% would indicate that nearly all diabetes cases in the high-intake group were due to sugar consumption, which is not supported by an RR of 3.0.

pages.question: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his aunt due to a sudden change in attitude over the past few weeks. He is having nightmares, seems more withdrawn at school, and has started to isolate himself from friends. The aunt notes that he appears visibly anxious about returning home after school. The boy lives with his uncle who has recently lost his job and has been facing financial difficulties. For years, the boy has been known to be boastful about his good grades, but he recently received a failing report card. When you inquire about his home life, the boy hesitates, avoids eye contact, and fidgets nervously. His aunt is worried about his deteriorating school performance and behavior. Who should you prioritize considering in this scenario?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The constellation of acute behavioral changes, anxiety about returning home, and declining academic performance in a financially stressed household raises immediate concern for physical abuse. Red flags include the child's avoidance behaviors during questioning and visible distress about the home environment. Child protective evaluation takes priority over other psychiatric diagnoses.
(Choice A)
Physical abuse
Given the boy's behavioral changes and the unstable home environment, it's critical to investigate possible physical abuse as a priority before other diagnoses.
(Choice B)
Generalized anxiety disorder
Although the child exhibits anxiety symptoms (nightmares, withdrawal, nervousness), these could be secondary to abuse. In pediatric cases with acute behavioral changes and home environment concerns, ruling out abuse takes precedence over primary anxiety disorders.
(Choice C)
Conduct disorder
Conduct disorder involves persistent patterns of violating social norms and others' rights. This child's symptoms (withdrawal, anxiety, academic decline) suggest trauma response rather than antisocial behavior patterns typical of conduct disorder.
(Choice D)
Psychological neglect
While psychological neglect can present with behavioral changes and withdrawal, the acute onset of symptoms combined with anxiety about returning home in a financially stressed household requires immediate evaluation for physical abuse before considering neglect.
(Choice E)
Avoidant personality disorder
Avoidant personality disorder is not diagnosed in children under 18 years of age. Additionally, the acute onset of symptoms suggests a situational stressor rather than a personality disorder pattern.

pages.question: A 35-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of poorly localized pain on the lateral aspect of her right knee. She recently started a high-intensity interval training program that includes repetitive squats, lunges, and hill sprints, as she is preparing for her first obstacle course race. The pain worsens during workouts and improves with rest, but she notes a snapping sensation over the lateral knee during knee flexion. On examination, there is tenderness just proximal to the lateral joint line, near the lateral femoral epicondyle. Applying pressure over this area while flexing the knee from 0 to 30 degrees reproduces her pain. There is no joint effusion, instability, or pain with varus/valgus stress. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Iliotibial band syndrome presents as poorly localized lateral knee pain with tenderness proximal to the lateral joint line near the lateral femoral epicondyle, commonly in individuals starting new or strenuous lower body training regimens like high-intensity interval training. Other conditions such as lateral collateral ligament sprain, lateral meniscus tear, patellofemoral pain syndrome, and pes anserine bursitis have distinct clinical features and sites of tenderness.
(Choice A)
Iliotibial band syndrome
This patient's presentation of poorly localized lateral knee pain, triggered by new repetitive lower body exercises, with tenderness proximal to the lateral joint line and pain reproduction on flexion under pressure, is characteristic of iliotibial band syndrome, caused by friction of the IT band over the lateral femoral epicondyle.
(Choice B)
Lateral collateral ligament injury
Lateral collateral ligament injury typically presents with pain and instability on varus stress testing, often following acute trauma or hyperextension injury, with tenderness directly over the ligament at the joint line rather than proximal to it, and without the characteristic snapping sensation during flexion seen in IT band syndrome.
(Choice C)
Patellofemoral pain syndrome
Patellofemoral pain syndrome features anterior knee pain worsened by activities loading the patellofemoral joint, such as stair climbing, with tenderness over the patella or retinaculum, not lateral tenderness proximal to the joint line.
(Choice D)
Pes anserine bursitis
Pes anserine bursitis causes medial knee pain and tenderness over the pes anserine insertion on the anteromedial proximal tibia, approximately 2-3 cm distal and medial to the joint line, commonly seen in overweight middle-aged women or patients with osteoarthritis, and does not present with lateral symptoms or snapping sensations.
(Choice E)
Lateral meniscus tear
Lateral meniscus tear usually causes pain localized to the lateral joint line with mechanical symptoms like locking, catching, or giving way, positive McMurray test, and often results from a twisting injury with the foot planted, rather than the repetitive overuse pattern and proximal tenderness described in this case.

pages.question:
A 32-year-old male graduate student presents with a 4-month history of recurrent crampy abdominal pain in the lower quadrants, which typically improves after defecation. He reports having bowel movements only 2-3 times per week, with hard, pellet-like stools that require straining. He denies any weight loss, rectal bleeding, fever, or family history of colon cancer. His physical examination is unremarkable, and laboratory tests are shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in management?



Hemoglobin	13.5 g/dL
Hematocrit	41%
White blood cell count	7600 /mm³
Platelet count	230000 /μL
Mean corpuscular volume	92 fL
Thyroid-stimulating hormone	2.1 μIU/mL
Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA	Negative
Total serum IgA	Normal
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has symptoms consistent with constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-C). In the absence of alarm features or laboratory abnormalities, further diagnostic testing such as colonoscopy is unnecessary. Initial management should include reassurance, dietary modifications, and a trial of fiber supplementation.
(Choice A)
Abdominal CT scan
Abdominal CT scan is not indicated for functional bowel disorders like IBS in the absence of alarm features. CT would not provide useful diagnostic information for IBS and exposes the patient to unnecessary radiation and healthcare costs.
(Choice B)
Referral for cognitive behavioral therapy
While psychological therapies including cognitive behavioral therapy can be beneficial for IBS management, they are typically reserved for patients who do not respond to first-line dietary and lifestyle interventions, or for those with significant psychosocial comorbidities.
(Choice C)
Trial of fiber supplementation
Fiber supplementation is appropriate first-line management for constipation-predominant IBS to improve stool frequency and consistency.
(Choice D)
Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy is not indicated in a 32-year-old patient without alarm features (weight loss, rectal bleeding, anemia, family history of colorectal cancer). Current guidelines recommend colonoscopy screening starting at age 45 for average-risk individuals, or earlier only in the presence of concerning symptoms or risk factors.
(Choice E)
Antispasmodic medication
Antispasmodics like dicyclomine or hyoscyamine primarily address abdominal cramping and pain but do not improve constipation. For IBS-C, addressing the constipation component with fiber supplementation takes priority as it can improve both stool frequency and associated cramping.

pages.question: A 62-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis presents for follow-up. She has had an inadequate response to methotrexate and a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor. The physician prescribes abatacept, an intravenous medication that targets T-cell costimulation, which is expected to improve her symptoms with a favorable side effect profile given her comorbidities. However, the patient's insurance company denies coverage, stating that a less expensive oral disease-modifying antirheumatic drug is preferred. The patient cannot afford the out-of-pocket cost. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text:
Provide medication samples from the office supply
(2.11%)

Advise the patient to pay for the medication out-of-pocket
(1.05%)

Refer the patient to a social worker for financial assistance programs
(32.63%)

Switch to the insurance-preferred oral antirheumatic drug
(2.11%)

Contact the insurance company to request prior authorization
(62.11%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has severe rheumatoid arthritis that has been refractory to methotrexate and TNF inhibitor therapy. Abatacept, a T-cell costimulation inhibitor, is clinically appropriate for refractory RA but was denied by insurance due to cost preferences. The most appropriate initial step is to contact the insurance company for prior authorization, providing medical justification for why abatacept is necessary given the patient's treatment history. This approach works within the insurance system while advocating for optimal patient care. Alternative options like switching to preferred medications, using samples, or seeking financial assistance may be considered later if prior authorization fails, but should not precede the systematic approach of working with the insurer.
(Choice A)
Provide medication samples from the office supply
While samples may provide temporary relief, they are not a sustainable long-term solution for chronic rheumatoid arthritis management. Additionally, samples do not address the underlying insurance coverage issue that needs to be resolved for ongoing therapy.
(Choice B)
Advise the patient to pay for the medication out-of-pocket
This is inappropriate because the patient has explicitly stated they cannot afford the out-of-pocket cost, making this option financially unfeasible and potentially harmful to the patient-physician relationship.
(Choice C)
Refer the patient to a social worker for financial assistance programs
While social work referral for patient assistance programs may be valuable as an adjunctive measure, it should not be the first step. The physician should first attempt to work within the insurance system through prior authorization, as this addresses the coverage denial directly and may provide a more reliable long-term solution.
(Choice D)
Switch to the insurance-preferred oral antirheumatic drug
Switching to the insurance-preferred medication without attempting prior authorization is premature and potentially suboptimal. The patient has already failed methotrexate and a TNF inhibitor, suggesting refractory disease that may not respond to another conventional DMARD. The physician should first advocate for the clinically appropriate medication through proper channels.
(Choice E)
Contact the insurance company to request prior authorization
Prior authorization involves providing additional medical justification to the insurer for approval of the denied medication, which is appropriate here as abatacept is indicated for this patient's refractory rheumatoid arthritis.

pages.question: A 42-year-old male welder with a 25-pack-year smoking history presents with recurrent episodes of pallor, cyanosis, and pain in his fingers and toes triggered by cold exposure or stress. He reports recent development of small, painful ulcers on the tips of his second and third fingers of the right hand, and intermittent rest pain in his right foot. He denies any skin tightening, joint pains, or systemic symptoms like fever or weight loss. Physical examination reveals asymmetric involvement with reduced pulses in the right radial and dorsalis pedis arteries, while the left side is normal. Laboratory tests show normal complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and antinuclear antibody screen. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient presents with asymmetric Raynaud phenomenon, digital ulcers, and a significant smoking history, raising suspicion for secondary Raynaud due to thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease). Arteriogram is the best next step to evaluate for characteristic vascular occlusions and corkscrew collaterals.
(Choice A)
Antinuclear antibody testing
ANA testing helps screen for autoimmune causes of secondary Raynaud, such as lupus or scleroderma, but the question states that ANA screen was already performed and was normal. Given the asymmetric presentation with ischemic features and smoking history, further vascular imaging is more appropriate than repeating autoimmune workup.
(Choice B)
Arteriogram
Arteriogram is the gold standard for diagnosing Buerger disease, showing characteristic multifocal occlusions and collateral vessels in affected limbs, which fits this patient's presentation of secondary Raynaud with ischemic features.
(Choice C)
Smoking cessation counseling alone
While smoking cessation is crucial in managing Buerger disease, it is not a diagnostic step; further imaging is needed to confirm the etiology in this patient with progressive ischemic symptoms.
(Choice D)
Nailfold capillaroscopy
Nailfold capillaroscopy is useful for detecting microvascular changes in connective tissue diseases like systemic sclerosis and distinguishing primary from secondary Raynaud. However, in this case with asymmetric presentation, digital ulcers, reduced pulses, and strong smoking history suggestive of macrovascular disease, arteriography is more appropriate to evaluate for large vessel occlusions characteristic of Buerger disease.
(Choice E)
Initiate calcium channel blocker therapy
Calcium channel blockers are a first-line treatment for primary Raynaud phenomenon, but in suspected secondary cases with ulcers and ischemia, diagnostic evaluation for underlying vascular disease takes precedence over empirical therapy.

pages.question: A third-year internal medicine resident is seeing four patients in clinic and must counsel each on lifespan-appropriate nutritional requirements. Patient A is a 14-year-old male athlete asking about nutrition for bone health. Patient B is a 29-year-old woman who just learned she is six weeks pregnant and has not been taking any supplements. Patient C is a 35-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding and fatigue asking whether she needs iron. Patient D is a 78-year-old man with a recent hip fracture, limited sun exposure, and a diet low in dairy. Which of the following correctly matches each patient to their most urgently needed nutritional intervention?

answers.text:
Patient A: vitamin D 4,000 IU/day high-dose therapy to maximize calcium absorption during pubertal growth; Patient B: initiate prenatal vitamins with reassurance that folic acid timing is not critical after conception; Patient C: restrict dietary iron sources to prevent overabsorption during heavy menstrual periods; Patient D: caloric restriction to reduce weight-bearing stress on fragile bones
(0%)

Patient A: iron supplementation for exercise-induced anemia; Patient B: no supplements needed as neural tube development is complete by six weeks; Patient C: vitamin B12 supplementation for anemia from menstrual blood loss; Patient D: protein restriction to reduce metabolic acid load and improve calcium balance
(0%)

Patient A: calcium 1,300 mg/day and vitamin D 600 IU/day for peak bone mass accrual; Patient B: folic acid 400–800 mcg/day immediately and counseling that neural tube closure may have already occurred; Patient C: iron evaluation with CBC and ferritin, supplementation if deficient; Patient D: calcium 1,200 mg/day and vitamin D 800–1,000 IU/day for fracture risk reduction
(100%)

Patient A: protein supplementation 2.0 g/kg/day for athletic performance; Patient B: vitamin A 5,000 IU/day for embryonic development; Patient C: calcium supplementation for menstrual symptom relief; Patient D: dietary cholesterol restriction to reduce cardiovascular risk
(0%)

Patient A: omega-3 fatty acid supplementation for exercise recovery support; Patient B: magnesium supplementation for preeclampsia prevention; Patient C: hormonal contraception as primary treatment for iron deficiency from heavy bleeding; Patient D: fiber supplementation to enhance calcium absorption in older adults
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This integrative question requires applying age- and sex-specific nutrient requirements across the lifespan. Adolescents need calcium 1,300 mg and vitamin D for peak bone mass. Pregnant women need folic acid urgently (though at six weeks neural tube closure may have already occurred, supplementation should begin immediately and dietary counseling provided). Premenopausal women with heavy menstrual bleeding need iron evaluation and supplementation. Older adults with fracture need calcium 1,200 mg and vitamin D 800–1,000 IU daily.
(Choice A)
Patient A: vitamin D 4,000 IU/day high-dose therapy to maximize calcium absorption during pubertal growth; Patient B: initiate prenatal vitamins with reassurance that folic acid timing is not critical after conception; Patient C: restrict dietary iron sources to prevent overabsorption during heavy menstrual periods; Patient D: caloric restriction to reduce weight-bearing stress on fragile bones
Vitamin D megadosing at 4,000 IU/day in an adolescent without confirmed deficiency risks toxicity and exceeds the tolerable upper intake level. Folic acid timing is highly relevant — neural tube closure at days 21–28 post-conception is the critical window, not the date of a positive pregnancy test. Heavy menstrual bleeding causes iron loss and deficiency, not iron overload — restricting iron sources would worsen the deficiency. Caloric restriction in an older adult with a hip fracture risks further muscle wasting, sarcopenia, micronutrient deficiency, and impaired fracture healing — the opposite of appropriate nutritional management.
(Choice B)
Patient A: iron supplementation for exercise-induced anemia; Patient B: no supplements needed as neural tube development is complete by six weeks; Patient C: vitamin B12 supplementation for anemia from menstrual blood loss; Patient D: protein restriction to reduce metabolic acid load and improve calcium balance
Each recommendation contains a critical error. Exercise-induced hemolysis causing anemia requires evaluation before empiric iron supplementation and is not the primary nutritional priority for a healthy adolescent athlete — calcium and vitamin D for bone health are. Folic acid should still be initiated at six weeks even if neural tube closure has occurred, as it supports ongoing pregnancy nutrition. Menstrual losses cause iron deficiency anemia (microcytic), not vitamin B12 deficiency (macrocytic). Protein restriction in an older adult with a hip fracture would worsen sarcopenia and increase fall and re-fracture risk — the opposite of the correct intervention.
(Choice C)
Patient A: calcium 1,300 mg/day and vitamin D 600 IU/day for peak bone mass accrual; Patient B: folic acid 400–800 mcg/day immediately and counseling that neural tube closure may have already occurred; Patient C: iron evaluation with CBC and ferritin, supplementation if deficient; Patient D: calcium 1,200 mg/day and vitamin D 800–1,000 IU/day for fracture risk reduction
This question integrates lifespan nutritional requirements across four distinct clinical scenarios. Patient A (14-year-old male athlete): Adolescence is the period of peak bone mass accrual, with 40–60% of adult bone mineral deposited during puberty. The recommended calcium intake is 1,300 mg/day (highest of any age group) and vitamin D 600 IU/day, achievable through dairy, fortified foods, and supplementation if dietary intake is inadequate. Athletic adolescents have additional calcium needs from sweat losses. Patient B (29-year-old, 6 weeks pregnant): Neural tube closure occurs at days 21–28 post-conception, meaning it has likely already completed at six weeks. However, folic acid 400–800 mcg/day should be initiated immediately as it remains important for placental development, red cell production, and prevention of other congenital anomalies throughout the first trimester. Iron (27 mg/day in pregnancy), iodine (220 mcg/day), and DHA supplementation should also be addressed. Patient C (35-year-old with heavy menstrual bleeding): Premenopausal women require 18 mg iron daily; heavy menstrual bleeding significantly increases losses. CBC and ferritin should guide supplementation decisions. Patient D (78-year-old with hip fracture): Older adults require calcium 1,200 mg/day and vitamin D 800–1,000 IU/day given reduced intestinal absorption efficiency, reduced cutaneous synthesis, and secondary hyperparathyroidism contributing to fracture risk. His recent hip fracture also warrants pharmacologic osteoporosis therapy evaluation.
(Choice D)
Patient A: protein supplementation 2.0 g/kg/day for athletic performance; Patient B: vitamin A 5,000 IU/day for embryonic development; Patient C: calcium supplementation for menstrual symptom relief; Patient D: dietary cholesterol restriction to reduce cardiovascular risk
Each of these recommendations is incorrect for the specific lifespan nutritional priorities of each patient. High-dose protein supplementation is not the priority for adolescent bone health — calcium and vitamin D are. Vitamin A supplementation in pregnancy carries teratogenicity risk above 10,000 IU/day and is not the urgent first-trimester intervention — folic acid is. Calcium does not prevent menstrual cramps and does not address the likely iron deficiency from heavy menstrual bleeding. Dietary cholesterol restriction is not the priority nutritional intervention for an older adult with a recent hip fracture — calcium and vitamin D for fracture risk reduction are the evidence-based priority.
(Choice E)
Patient A: omega-3 fatty acid supplementation for exercise recovery support; Patient B: magnesium supplementation for preeclampsia prevention; Patient C: hormonal contraception as primary treatment for iron deficiency from heavy bleeding; Patient D: fiber supplementation to enhance calcium absorption in older adults
While omega-3 fatty acids have anti-inflammatory properties, they are not the primary lifespan nutritional priority for adolescent bone health. Magnesium supplementation for preeclampsia prevention is not evidence-based as a nutritional intervention — intravenous magnesium sulfate is used therapeutically for eclampsia seizure prevention, not dietary supplementation prenatally. Oral contraceptives can reduce menstrual blood loss and are a valid gynecological intervention, but the question asks about nutritional interventions, and assessment of iron status with supplementation if deficient is the appropriate nutritional approach. Dietary fiber does not meaningfully improve calcium absorption in the aging colon — reduced VDR expression and impaired renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity are the primary mechanisms of age-related calcium malabsorption requiring vitamin D supplementation.

pages.question: A 75-year-old man with a history of osteoporosis presents to the emergency department after slipping on ice while walking his dog. He complains of intense pain in his left hip and is unable to stand or walk. Physical examination reveals that his left leg is shortened and externally rotated compared to the right leg, with significant tenderness in the groin area. There is no history of high-impact trauma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This elderly man with osteoporosis has an acutely shortened, externally rotated leg following a low-impact fall, consistent with a femoral neck fracture, one of the most common hip fractures in older adults due to mechanical falls. The classic presentation of shortening and external rotation results from unopposed contraction of the iliopsoas muscle. Posterior hip dislocation typically causes internal rotation without shortening. Femoral shaft fractures often present with thigh deformity but not external rotation. Pubic ramus fractures usually do not alter leg length or rotation. Greater trochanter fractures may cause pain but do not typically shorten or rotate the leg.
(Choice A)
Femoral shaft fracture
This is incorrect; femoral shaft fractures cause mid-thigh pain, swelling, and deformity but do not typically result in the classic external rotation and significant shortening seen with hip fractures.
(Choice B)
Posterior hip dislocation
This is incorrect; posterior hip dislocations typically present with leg shortening and internal rotation (not external rotation), and usually result from high-energy trauma such as motor vehicle accidents, not low-impact falls in the elderly.
(Choice C)
Greater trochanter fracture
This is incorrect; isolated greater trochanter fractures cause lateral hip pain and tenderness but do not affect leg length or cause external rotation.
(Choice D)
Pubic ramus fracture
This is incorrect; pubic ramus fractures are common in elderly patients after falls and cause groin pain, but patients typically retain the ability to bear weight (though painful) and do not develop leg shortening or external rotation.
(Choice E)
Femoral neck fracture
This is the correct diagnosis, as the clinical findings of leg shortening and external rotation after a fall in an older adult are classic for femoral neck or intertrochanteric fractures, commonly due to low-energy trauma in osteoporotic bone.
